meta.title: Coercive Control Appeal Tracker
meta.sourceNote: CourtListener search of United States opinions that use the words coercive control. The list keeps one published card per case. Research, not legal advice.
method: A published opinion that names coercive control does not finish the work.
The hard part is showing the pattern in a longitudinal record.
Carlton Research, LLC does not represent parties and does not make parenting-time recommendations.
CourtListener supplies the list. The list updates automatically.

cases.title: Marriage of Traweek
cases.summary: Scott Traweek appealed the spousal support award after Candice Traweek rebutted the Family Code section 4325 presumption against support to a spouse convicted of domestic violence. The Court of Appeal affirmed. The trial court treated Scott's concealment and withholding of income as coercive control under Family Code section 6320(c)(3) and weighed that abuse as an equitable factor. The court limited Candice's recovery by denying retroactive support and an Ostler-Smith share of overtime, and by setting a non-modifiable termination date. Certified for publication.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.title: Lopez v. United States
cases.summary: Before trial, the government notified Lopez of its intent to introduce the testimony of Raghavan as an expert in “traumatic bonding and coercive control in the context of domestic violence.” The government argued that Raghavan’s testimony would help explain “paradoxical, incongruous behavior by the victim [of an abuser] that is often hard for a lay person, like a juror, to understand.” Raghavan also proposed to explain how and “why a relationship may become more lethal” when the victim “successfully ends the relationship with the abuser.” Lopez moved to exclude this testimony on several grounds, including that it appeared to be rank propensity evidence.

cases.title: O'Neal v. Reeves
cases.summary: The trial court erred by disregarding Appellant’s evidence of post-divorce financial abuse, including unauthorized credit use in Ohio and Georgia, which constituted ongoing contempt and coercive control. Appellee’s misconduct was further compounded following the July 14, 2025, purge order, where the minimal sanction of $25.70 failed to deter noncompliance.

cases.title: Marriage of G.E. & I.D.
cases.summary: Wife appealed dismissal of her domestic violence restraining order petition and termination of a temporary order mid-hearing, after testimony that Husband struck her and the child, threatened to kill them, threatened deportation, and strictly controlled finances and social relationships. The Court of Appeal reversed and remanded with instructions to reinstate the temporary order and continue the petition hearing. The opinion applied Family Code section 6320, including coercive control as a pattern that in purpose or effect unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and personal liberty. Certified for publication.

cases.title: Sreya Vuth, V. Mehran Tavakoli
cases.summary: Vuth appealed partial summary judgment that limited her intentional infliction of emotional distress claim to the three-year limitations window. The Court of Appeals reversed and remanded. RCW 7.105 defines domestic violence to include coercive control, a pattern of behavior that unreasonably interferes with free will and personal liberty. On the complaint's alleged facts, the court described Tavakoli's coercive control as glaringly obvious and held the continuing-tort doctrine applies to those claims when domestic violence is a continuing course of conduct. Published opinion.

cases.title: P.C. v. G.S.
cases.summary: The Court did not find that Father exerted extreme psychological abuse and/or coercive control over Mother, notwithstanding Mother's allegations. Furthermore, the Court did not find any merit as to Mother's allegations that Father was abusive towards the children, and did not include the children on the Order for Protection filed 7/15/2024.

cases.title: Aiden Asbach v. Adam Couto
cases.summary: Couto appealed domestic violence protection orders protecting Karina Asbach and Aiden Asbach, plus attorney fees on renewal of a third order. The trial court found Couto's YouTube videos were a form of coercive control under RCW 7.105 and ordered removal of videos naming the protected persons. The Court of Appeals affirmed the protection orders and fee awards, granted appellate attorney fees to Karina and Aiden, and remanded to modify the prohibition against posting videos and other media.

cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court Appellate Division
cases.title: G.G.S. v. A.C.B.
cases.summary: G.G.S. appealed denial of a final restraining order after the trial court credited testimony of forcible sexual assault and strangulation. The Appellate Division reversed and remanded for entry of a final restraining order. Strangulation was treated as coercive control and domination that the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act is designed to forestall. N.J.S.A. 2C:25-29(a)(7) requires courts to consider any pattern of coercive control. Once the credited facts were found, the need for a final restraining order was treated as self-evident under Silver.

cases.title: Marriage of Hoch
cases.summary: Both spouses appealed. The Court of Appeal affirmed the domestic violence restraining order against Michael and reversed the mutual order against Marcie. Michael's free-exercise challenge failed as to the order grounded in coercive control: tracking whereabouts, accessing electronic devices and online accounts, monitoring reading material, restricting movement, and appearing uninvited. Harassment, annoyance, and coercive control can support an order without a showing of fear. Certified for publication.

cases.title: D.S. v. W.G.
cases.summary: DS appealed denial of an HRS chapter 586 order for protection. The Intermediate Court of Appeals affirmed. New 2023 allegations, including inquiries concerning an ex-wife and daughter and a message through a third party, did not establish extreme psychological abuse or an alternative form of abuse including coercive control as defined in HRS 586-1. Issues from a prior proceeding were barred by res judicata. Summary disposition, not for publication.

cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court Appellate Division
cases.title: S.M.T. v. S.A.
cases.summary: The parties appealed denials of final restraining orders against each other. S.M.T. alleged physical abuse, forced sexual acts, and coercive control. The trial court found simple assault but treated much of the history as marital contretemps and denied an order. The Appellate Division reversed in part and remanded for entry of a final restraining order in favor of S.M.T., holding she proved simple assault, sexual assault, and coercive control and established a likelihood of continued domestic violence. Coercive control is a Silver factor under N.J.S.A. 2C:25-29(a)(7), not a predicate act. Denial of S.A.'s order was affirmed. Approved for publication.

cases.title: R.R. v. C.R.
cases.summary: R.R. appealed denial of a domestic violence restraining order against his former spouse. The Court of Appeal reversed and remanded with directions to enter the order. The trial court misapplied the Domestic Violence Prevention Act. Family Code section 6320 covers stalking, harassment, and disturbing the peace, including coercive control such as monitoring movements. Past abuse, which the trial court called alarming, sufficed. A showing of probable future abuse was not required. Certified for publication.

cases.summary: The PTE explained that Parents’ relationship was marked with coercive control dynamics, which tend to maintain ongoing higher levels of conflict. cases.title: People v. Uddin
cases.summary: At trial, the People proffered an expert "in the field of domestic violence, coercive control, trauma, and the cultural impact of them." The defendant did not object. In any event, the contention is without merit, as the expert demonstrated through her foundational testimony that she possessed the skill, training, knowledge, and experience necessary to proffer an opinion ( see De Long v County of Erie , 60 NY2d 296, 307; People v Flores , 153 AD3d 182, 196, affd 32 NY3d 1087) about the delay in outcry common to domestic violence victims, including victims of sexual assault, as well as the impact of culture on outcry ( see People v Williams , 20 NY3d 579; People v Khalil , 206 AD3d 1300).

cases.summary: It stated that while the circumstances surrounding the signing of the agreement “suggest that [Julie] was an unequal bargaining partner , had little time to consider whether to enter into the agreement, did not negotiate any terms, and was repeatedly told by [Steve] that he would take care of her, she did understand what she was signing and exercised a choice .” The court also found that although Steve had committed one act of domestic violence against Julie a year before the signing of the prenuptial agreement, Julie’s decision to sign did not appear to be “the product of coercive control.” In applying the second step, the court found that the terms of the agreement were not so unconscionable as to make the prenuptial agreement entirely unenforceable.

cases.title: D. A. v. A. C.
cases.summary: The defendant appealed a protective order and the denial of a motion to dismiss. The Appellate Court affirmed. The plaintiff's testimony, with that of the guardian ad litem, established a prima facie case of domestic violence under section 46b-1(b), which includes coercive control. The defendant relied on a superseded revision of section 46b-15 and left stalking and coercive control unchallenged.

RCW 7.105.010(4)(a) does not require a finding of intent; the effect of the pattern can suffice. Later ordered published.

cases.citation: 232 Conn. App. 434, 337 A.3d 14, cert. denied, 353 Conn. 902 (2025)
cases.summary: The plaintiff appealed after the trial court denied a domestic violence restraining order. The Appellate Court applied a broader definition of coercive control under section 46b-1(b)(4) than the trial court used: the statutory examples are not an exclusive list. Even if conduct while the parties lived together amounted to coercive control, that coercive control had ended by the time of the application. The plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case under section 46b-1(b)(4). The form of judgment was reversed and the case remanded with direction to dismiss under Practice Book section 15-8.

cases.title: Marriage of L.R. and K.A.
cases.summary: Mother appealed a three-year domestic violence restraining order issued after an urgent-care custody clash that the responding officer described as a child custody dispute. The Court of Appeal reversed and directed denial of the order. Applying Family Code section 6320, including the coercive control definition and its legislative guardrails, the court held Mother's conduct showed poor co-parenting but did not destroy Father's mental and emotional calm within the meaning of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act. Certified for publication.
